questions.title: Why does section 552(a)(4)(F)(i) not limit OSC’s authority under section 1216(a)(3) for FOIA investigations?
questions.question_body: The opinion says that the district court found that “s 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC’s power to investigate alleged FOIA violations under section 1216.” I thought the three predicates in 552(a)(4)(F)(i) were prerequisites for any OSC enforcement action. How can OSC still investigate under 1216 if those predicates are missing?

questions.title: What is the difference between a procedural injury and a substantive injury under the relaxed standing standard?
questions.question_body: The court talks about a relaxed standing requirement for procedural injuries but says AFL fails even that standard. I’m confused about the line between a procedural right‑in‑vacuo and a substantive injury, and why the court concluded that preventing OSC from investigating does not amount to a concrete injury.

questions.title: Why is the causal chain from OSC’s inaction to DOJ’s FOIA compliance considered too speculative?
questions.question_body: The opinion outlines a multi‑legislative causal chain involving OSC, the Merit Systems Protection Board, and DOJ. The court calls it speculative. Could someone explain why the court doesn’t allow speculation about the actions of independent agencies when determining standing?

questions.title: How does the court determine that an informational injury from a FOIA request is not concrete or particularized?
questions.question_body: AFL argues that not receiving the documents is an injury. The court rejects it, citing that an informational injury is not concrete. What factors make an informational interest concrete or not under Article III standing?

questions.title: In what ways is a plaintiff’s request for OSC to investigate a FOIA policy equivalent to or different from a FOIA request for records?
questions.question_body: AFL sought OSC’s investigation of DOJ’s policy that it does not search employee emails without consent. How does that differ from a typical FOIA claim for records, and why does that distinction matter for standing?

questions.title: What does it mean for an OSC investigation under §1216 to be discretionary versus mandatory?
questions.question_body: The opinion says OSC’s decision whether to follow §1214 notice requirements is discretionary in a §1216 investigation. Could someone elaborate on what is mandatory here and what OSC can decide, and how that affects a plaintiff’s claim?

questions.title: Does OSC’s refusal to investigate create an entitlement to receive notice or information under §1214?
questions.question_body: AFL contends that if OSC were required to investigate, it would have to give it the same notices that would come in a §1214 investigation. Is there any legal basis that an investigation under §1216 creates a right to those §1214 notices, or is it purely discretionary?

questions.title: How does the Supreme Court’s treatment of ‘redressability’ in the context of discretionary enforcement tools impact standing analysis?
questions.question_body: The opinion references decisions that redressability focuses on the judgment’s effect on the parties, not on speculative future actions by other agencies. Could someone explain how that principle shapes the court’s conclusion that AFL cannot be redressed by a ruling to force OSC to investigate?
